questions.stem: A healthy patient completed a phone preanesthesia interview 12 days ago. The chart is complete and nothing has changed. Which requirement still cannot be omitted on the morning of surgery?
options: A repeat interview only if laboratory values changed
No further interview because the phone assessment remains valid
An in-person clinic interview because the prior assessment was remote
questions.explanation: The preoperative assessment can occur 1–30 days ahead, including by phone, but a day-of-surgery interview is still required.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A healthy patient cannot attend an in-person preoperative clinic but can complete a structured phone assessment. Which plan preserves the intended preoperative process?
options: Complete the assessment within the accepted preoperative window, then repeat a focused interview on the day of surgery
Delay all assessment until the morning of surgery
Require an in-person clinic visit solely because the interview is remote
Use the phone assessment as a substitute for all day-of-surgery reassessment
questions.explanation: The preoperative assessment window is 1–30 days before surgery, followed by a day-of-surgery interview.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: An elective colectomy patient has EF 25%, stage 4 CKD, and insulin-dependent diabetes but is not acutely decompensated. What timing best preserves an opportunity for optimization rather than merely identifying risk on the day of surgery?
options: At least a week before surgery
Any time within 30 days if symptoms develop
questions.explanation: Medically complex patients should visit the preop testing center at least a week before surgery so testing and optimization can happen and preventable cancellations are avoided.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A hospital is deciding whether an in-person preoperative testing clinic adds value beyond a day-of-surgery interview. Which benefits justify the clinic? (Select 4)
options: Consolidated testing such as labs, imaging, and other studies
Time to optimize medical conditions before surgery
Replacement of the surgeon's history and physical
questions.explanation: Early visits educate, consolidate testing, allow optimization, and reduce preventable cancellations. They do not replace the day-of interview or the surgeon's H&P.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A 66-year-old takes metoprolol, lisinopril, furosemide, and glipizide. To avoid rebound sympathetic effects without increasing common peri-induction medication risks, which drug should be taken with a sip of water?
questions.explanation: Beta-blockers are continued to avoid rebound tachycardia and ischemia. ACE inhibitors, diuretics, and oral hypoglycemics are held.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient takes losartan, amlodipine, and hydrochlorothiazide. Which morning-of-surgery plan best avoids medication-related hypotension or volume depletion while maintaining usual antihypertensive therapy?
options: Take amlodipine; hold losartan and hydrochlorothiazide
Take losartan; hold amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide
Take hydrochlorothiazide and amlodipine; hold losartan
questions.explanation: Most antihypertensives are taken, but ARBs, ACE inhibitors, and diuretics are held. Losartan and HCTZ are held; amlodipine is taken.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A 68-year-old takes lisinopril 40 mg every morning, including today, and is induced with propofol 150 mg. BP falls to 68/35 and responds only briefly to phenylephrine. What mechanism BEST explains this?
options: Lisinopril causes direct myocardial depression with propofol
Lisinopril causes hyperkalemia that depresses contractility
questions.explanation: With the renin-angiotensin system blocked, the patient cannot compensate for anesthetic vasodilation, so hypotension is refractory to standard pressors. This is why ACE inhibitors and ARBs are commonly held.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: One patient has a drug-eluting coronary stent and takes aspirin plus clopidogrel; another takes rivaroxaban for atrial fibrillation. Which management principle applies to both before surgery?
options: Individualize interruption or continuation by balancing bleeding and thrombosis
Continue both drug classes through surgery as a fixed rule
Hold both drug classes only on the morning of surgery as a fixed rule
Replace either regimen with low-dose aspirin the day before surgery
questions.explanation: Anticoagulants and antiplatelets are managed case by case, balancing surgical and neuraxial bleeding risk against thrombotic risk such as stent thrombosis.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient with Parkinson disease and a seizure disorder is NPO for surgery and asks whether carbidopa-levodopa and levetiracetam should be skipped. Which instruction best prevents avoidable perioperative deterioration?
options: Take both on the morning of surgery
Hold both to minimize anesthetic interactions
questions.explanation: Antiseizure and Parkinson's medications are on the "take" list. Stopping them risks seizures or rigidity and aspiration.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A 70-year-old takes furosemide, glyburide, a multivitamin, fish oil, an albuterol inhaler, and metoprolol. Which four are ordinarily held on the morning of surgery? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Hold diuretics, oral hypoglycemics, and vitamins or herbals. Inhalers and beta-blockers are taken.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient takes oxycodone 10 mg every 8 hours chronically and is scheduled for a painful laminectomy. Which morning-of-surgery instruction best limits withdrawal and worsening postoperative analgesic requirements?
options: Hold the dose to reduce intraoperative respiratory depression
Take half of the usual dose
Hold the dose and substitute only a postoperative PCA
questions.explanation: Home opioids are continued. Stopping them risks withdrawal and makes postoperative pain harder to control.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: Which preoperative action best reflects the purpose of evaluation rather than simply completing documentation?
options: Identify modifiable risk, prepare the patient, and build an anesthetic plan
Diagnose every untreated disease, order routine labs, and schedule surgery
Obtain consent, administer premedication, and start an IV
Assign ASA class, calculate one risk score, and determine staffing
questions.explanation: Preoperative evaluation aims to reduce risk and morbidity, prepare the patient medically and psychologically, and develop a comprehensive plan.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: You begin chart review for the first case of the day. Which verification comes before interpreting comorbidities, laboratory values, or prior anesthetic records?
options: Patient identity and the planned procedure
Risk stratification and the provisional anesthetic plan
The most recent laboratory values and imaging
questions.explanation: Chart review begins by confirming patient ID and procedure, then moves to history, prior anesthetic records, labs, risk, consent, allergies, and medications.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A prior anesthetic record documents a grade 4 laryngoscopic view with successful bougie-assisted video laryngoscopy. What should this finding change before induction?
options: Prepare a difficult-airway strategy and equipment in advance
Document it but begin with the usual airway plan
Use rapid-sequence induction with a Mac 4 blade as the default first attempt
Choose regional anesthesia solely to avoid airway management
questions.explanation: Identifying previous intubation notes and difficult airways is a chart review essential. It should drive equipment and plan, such as VL and the difficult airway cart.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A 72-year-old reports severe postoperative nausea and vomiting and two days of confusion after a prior anesthetic. Which additional anesthesia-history elements belong in the same focused review? (Select 4)
options: Personal or family history of malignant hyperthermia
questions.explanation: The anesthesia history covers difficult airway, PONV, emergence delirium or slow emergence, and personal or family history of MH.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient's father developed marked hyperthermia and muscle rigidity during anesthesia and nearly died. Which interpretation has the greatest anesthetic consequence?
options: This is anesthesia history suggesting possible familial malignant hyperthermia susceptibility
This is social history suggesting postoperative alcohol withdrawal risk
This is cardiac history predicting perioperative ischemia
This is family history primarily suggesting pseudocholinesterase deficiency
questions.explanation: Family history of MH is flagged in the anesthesia history section. It may require a trigger-free technique.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: The chart lists no prior anesthetic complications, but the patient recalls awakening after surgery, becoming severely dyspneic, and requiring reintubation. What is the most important lesson for the current evaluation?
options: Important anesthetic complications may be absent from the existing chart
The prior chart should no longer be used for planning
Patient recollection should replace review of previous records
The interview removes the need for formal consent
questions.explanation: The interview captures history and complications that may not be documented, and it verifies medications and allergies.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: One patient lists codeine as an allergy because of nausea and pruritus; another reports penicillin-associated hives and lip swelling. What distinction should be explicitly documented because it changes how each entry is interpreted?
questions.explanation: Allergy verification separates immune-mediated reactions (hives, angioedema) from non-immune side effects (nausea, itching from histamine release).
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: You have limited time for a focused day-of-surgery examination before an uncomplicated hernia repair. Which examination set is most aligned with anesthesia-specific risk detection?
options: Airway, neurologic, cardiovascular, pulmonary, and gastrointestinal
Airway, cardiovascular, renal, skin, and musculoskeletal
Neurologic, cardiovascular, endocrine, renal, and gastrointestinal
Airway, pulmonary, hematologic, renal, and skin
questions.explanation: The modified physical assessment includes airway, neuro, cardiovascular, pulmonary, and GI on the day of surgery.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient had a complete preoperative clinic examination two weeks ago but now reports new bilateral ankle swelling. What is required before induction?
options: A focused day-of-surgery physical addressing the interval change
No further examination because a full physical was already completed
A repeat complete physical only if laboratory values also changed
questions.explanation: The modified physical (airway, neuro, CV, pulmonary, GI) is done on the day of surgery, which is how new findings like edema are caught.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A healthy ambulatory patient has a responsible adult available to drive home after anesthesia, but no one can stay with the patient afterward. Which discharge-planning issue should be identified before proceeding?
options: No responsible adult is available for the first 24 hours after anesthesia
Transportation home is adequate, so no additional support is needed
A family member must be present during induction
The surgical consent requires a relative's signature
questions.explanation: The slide says ask who is present and who will be there to care for them at least 24 hours after anesthesia.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: The chart already documents OSA on CPAP, diabetes, and a previous difficult intubation. With limited preoperative interview time, which approach best reduces the chance of missing a new risk?
options: Verify the known high-risk findings, then deliberately probe for gaps or interval changes
Repeat the entire history without using the chart
Ask only about diagnoses already listed in the chart
Review abnormal chart items and omit questions about unchanged systems
questions.explanation: Covering known issues first, then probing for missing information, balances efficiency with completeness.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: An SRNA repeatedly omits important preoperative questions when cases become busy. Which change most directly reduces omission errors without replacing clinical judgment?
options: Use a consistent structured interview template
Use a scripted consent video before each case
Rely on the preoperative order set to capture the history
Substitute a patient questionnaire for the interview
questions.explanation: The preop interview takes practice, and a personal template early in training keeps it complete and consistent.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient appears guarded at the start of the preoperative interview. Which opening approach is most likely to improve disclosure without sacrificing professionalism?
options: Introduce yourself and your role, address the patient respectfully, and explain the purpose of the interview
Begin with rapid closed-ended questions before introducing yourself
Use an informal nickname from the chart to reduce distance
Delay explaining your role until consent is discussed
questions.explanation: The slide advises using the surname to show respect along with a professional attitude and introduction.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A 74-year-old takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation and is scheduled for total knee arthroplasty with a planned spinal. Which principle should drive the perioperative anticoagulation plan?
options: Balance thromboembolic risk against surgical and neuraxial bleeding risk
Continue apixaban through surgery because atrial fibrillation is chronic
Hold only the morning dose and proceed with spinal anesthesia
Replace apixaban with aspirin the day before surgery
questions.explanation: Anticoagulants are managed case by case. Timing must account for surgical bleeding, neuraxial hematoma risk, and thrombotic risk.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: Three weeks before elective hip replacement, a patient reports exertional chest pain and subsequent testing demonstrates inducible ischemia. Which function of the preoperative process is most clearly demonstrated?
options: Identifying a problem early enough for additional evaluation or optimization
Improving operating-room turnover by completing testing early
Replacing the surgeon's history and physical examination
Determining whether the patient can be discharged the same day
questions.explanation: Perioperative evaluation identifies patients who need further testing or optimization before surgery, reducing risk.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A fasting patient accidentally takes the usual morning glipizide dose before surgery. Which immediate preoperative risk should receive priority surveillance?
questions.explanation: Oral hypoglycemics are held because a fasting patient can become hypoglycemic. Check glucose and monitor.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A preoperative holding RN obtains an excellent history and airway screen. What remains necessary before anesthesia under the facility's stated assessment policy?
options: An authorized clinician such as an anesthesiologist, CRNA, NP, or PA must perform the formal preanesthesia assessment
The RN's assessment is sufficient for ASA I–II patients
A later cosign automatically converts the RN assessment into the formal assessment
Only the surgeon must review the RN assessment
questions.explanation: The preanesthesia assessment may be done by an MD, CRNA, NP, or PA, but not by an RN.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A chart carries a difficult-airway alert, but the patient cannot recall details. Which two chart elements are most important to review before finalizing the airway plan? (Select 2)
options: Current consent, allergies, and medication list
questions.explanation: Chart review covers ID, procedure, prior records including intubation notes, labs, risk stratification, consent, allergies, and medications.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient reports that after a prior anesthetic he became apneic in PACU and required prolonged respiratory support. Which preoperative interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Treat it as an anesthesia-history signal for conditions such as OSA or heightened respiratory-depressant sensitivity
Classify it only as a medication-history issue from benzodiazepine exposure
Classify it as social history suggesting substance misuse
Classify it as surgical history because it occurred after the operation
questions.explanation: Postop respiratory events are anesthesia history. They raise concern for OSA or opioid sensitivity and change monitoring and analgesia.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: An 81-year-old was confused and not at baseline for three days after a previous anesthetic. Where should this information be captured because it may alter the current anesthetic and recovery plan?
options: Prior anesthesia history, including postoperative delirium or delayed recovery
Medication history as an isolated opioid adverse effect
questions.explanation: Emergence delirium or slow emergence belongs in the anesthesia history, especially in elderly patients who are at higher risk.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient has never received anesthesia and reports no known drug allergies. How should this history affect planning?
options: Do not infer tolerance to anesthetic drugs from the absence of prior exposure; maintain standard readiness for unexpected reactions
Classify the patient as higher ASA status solely because anesthetic exposure is unknown
Avoid common anesthetic drugs because first exposure predicts allergy
Assume low reaction risk eliminates the need to verify allergy history
questions.explanation: The allergy slide says use caution with a patient who has never had anesthesia because reactions to common triggers are unknown.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: An 84-year-old with a mechanical mitral valve takes warfarin and presents with a hip fracture and INR 3.1. Which approach best reflects the competing perioperative risks?
options: Coordinate an individualized plan for reversal, timing, and thromboembolic protection
Continue warfarin unchanged and treat bleeding only if it occurs
Stop warfarin and proceed immediately without further planning
Replace warfarin with aspirin and proceed
questions.explanation: Anticoagulants are case by case. With a mechanical valve, reversal, bridging, and timing must be planned with the surgical and cardiology teams.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient was considered low risk three weeks ago, but this morning potassium is 6.1 mEq/L with new peaked T waves. What must the day-of-surgery review do first with the prior assessment?
options: Reassess whether the previous risk stratification and anesthetic plan remain valid
Confirm only that surgical consent is signed
Confirm NPO status and keep the prior plan unchanged
Accept the original plan because it was completed within 30 days
questions.explanation: Day-of-surgery chart review verifies that the risk stratification and plan are still valid; new hyperkalemia changes both.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: Which history should trigger the largest change in anesthetic preparation before an otherwise routine elective case?
options: A first-degree relative developed severe hyperthermia and rigidity during anesthesia
The patient had mild nausea after a previous dental anesthetic
The patient has seasonal allergic rhinitis
The patient had an uncomplicated appendectomy years ago
questions.explanation: A family history suggestive of MH requires a trigger-free anesthetic. The others may adjust the plan but do not change the technique.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient with atrial fibrillation misses the usual morning metoprolol dose and arrives with HR 118/min. Which consequence best explains why chronic beta-blocker therapy is ordinarily continued?
options: Loss of rate control with rebound sympathetic activity and greater myocardial oxygen demand
Prolonged neuromuscular blockade from beta-receptor upregulation
Refractory vasodilatory hypotension from beta-blocker withdrawal
Reduced MAC requirement from acute beta-blocker discontinuation
questions.explanation: Beta-blockers are taken to avoid withdrawal tachycardia and ischemia.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient consents to general anesthesia with an LMA after hearing only the planned technique; possible intubation and neuraxial alternatives were not discussed. Which element of informed consent is deficient?
options: Meaningful discussion of material risks and reasonable alternatives
The consent was signed after, rather than before, the discussion
Regional anesthesia is not an alternative that needs discussion
Airway risks are covered automatically by the surgical consent
questions.explanation: Informed consent requires discussing risks, benefits, and options, including alternatives such as neuraxial or regional techniques.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient with severe COPD is scheduled for total knee arthroplasty. Which anesthetic option deserves explicit discussion because it may reduce the need for airway instrumentation and systemic respiratory depressants?
options: General anesthesia because it is mandatory for knee surgery
Routine postoperative ICU admission regardless of technique
questions.explanation: The plan discussion should include neuraxial or regional options, which can avoid airway instrumentation in a patient with severe COPD.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: After evaluating a patient with OSA and coronary disease for colectomy, which three decisions belong directly in the anesthesia plan generated from the assessment? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: The preoperative assessment leads to a plan covering premedication, monitoring, positioning, and equipment setup.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient takes St. John's wort, ginkgo, and vitamin E before a spine procedure. Which instruction best addresses medication-interaction and bleeding concerns?
options: Hold the vitamins and herbal products before surgery
Continue all three to prevent withdrawal
Take half-doses on the morning of surgery
Continue ginkgo but hold St. John's wort and vitamin E
questions.explanation: Vitamins and herbals are held. Ginkgo and vitamin E can increase bleeding, and St. John's wort induces drug metabolism.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: During preoperative interview, a patient discloses hepatitis C and prior IV drug use that were not documented in the chart. Which risk-assessment function is most directly served by obtaining this history?
options: Identifying exposure-related risk relevant to both patient and perioperative team
Choosing which surgeon should perform the procedure
questions.explanation: The preop evaluation assesses risk to the patient and the provider, such as bloodborne pathogen exposure.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A guarded patient gives minimal answers until the anesthesia clinician introduces themself clearly, explains the purpose of the interview, and addresses the patient respectfully. Why can this change the quality of the assessment?
options: Improved trust increases the likelihood of a complete history and meaningful consent
A professional introduction shortens every interview regardless of complexity
Rapport eliminates the need to verify the chart
A courteous introduction substitutes for formal consent
questions.explanation: A respectful introduction builds trust, which improves the accuracy of the history and the quality of informed consent.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient is scheduled for ankle fixation under a popliteal block with minimal sedation. Which reason best justifies performing the same airway assessment used before general anesthesia?
options: Regional or MAC plans can fail or deepen, making unplanned airway rescue necessary
Any sedative dose automatically requires tracheal intubation
Airway findings determine the local anesthetic dose
Fracture surgery has a uniquely high regional-anesthesia failure rate
questions.explanation: Any anesthetic can progress to needing airway rescue, so the airway is evaluated for every patient.

questions.stem: A patient has Mallampati II, adequate mouth opening, a full beard, a short thick neck, and limited cervical extension. Which interpretation is most useful for planning?
options: Multiple modest predictors can combine to create difficult mask ventilation or laryngoscopy
Mallampati II makes the remaining findings clinically unimportant
The beard alone determines the airway plan
Limited neck extension alone determines the airway plan
questions.explanation: Several minor findings can combine to create difficulty with mask ventilation and laryngoscopy.

questions.stem: A patient with BMI 38, Mallampati III, a full beard, and a short neck requires general anesthesia. Which preparation best matches the combined airway findings without overcommitting to one technique?
options: Prepare optimized positioning, video laryngoscopy, and difficult-airway rescue equipment
Use only the standard airway setup because no single finding guarantees difficulty
Plan awake fiberoptic intubation for every patient with this combination
Delay surgery until the patient shaves the beard
questions.explanation: Anticipating a difficult airway means planning VL, positioning aids, and the difficult airway cart.

questions.stem: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis has limited cervical motion and is scheduled for general anesthesia. Which focused examination best characterizes the structures most relevant to mask ventilation and laryngoscopy?
options: Dentition/oral cavity, mandibular space, and cervical mobility
Sinuses, ears, chest wall, and abdomen
Pupils, tonsils, trachea, and lower-extremity reflexes
Skin, thyroid function, renal status, and gait
questions.explanation: The airway exam inspects the teeth, mouth, mandibular space, and neck.

questions.stem: A patient has acromegaly, another has a large goiter, and a third has Pierre Robin sequence. Why do these diagnoses matter during airway assessment?
options: Different systemic, structural, or congenital processes can alter airway anatomy and make ventilation or laryngoscopy difficult
Each diagnosis predicts the same airway problem and requires the same technique
Only the goiter is relevant because metabolic and congenital disease do not affect the airway
All three mandate awake intubation regardless of examination
questions.explanation: Airway problems fall into structural features, metabolic diseases, and congenital or acquired anomalies.

questions.stem: A patient with Parkinson disease is scheduled for surgery. Which preoperative finding is most important to establish as a neurologic baseline rather than treating it as a new postoperative complication later?
options: Usual tremor pattern and current antiparkinsonian medications
questions.explanation: The neuro slide lists CVA, Parkinson's, or essential tremor history. Baseline tremor and medications matter for planning.

questions.stem: A patient with epilepsy is scheduled for surgery. Which history provides the most useful basis for perioperative seizure-risk planning?
options: Seizure type, frequency, triggers, medications, and time of last event
Seizure classification alone because medications are in the chart
Medication list alone because triggers do not affect perioperative risk
questions.explanation: A useful seizure history includes type, frequency, triggers, medications, and the last episode.

questions.stem: A patient with a remote stroke is scheduled for carotid endarterectomy. Which preoperative neurologic documentation is most useful for distinguishing a new perioperative event from an old deficit?
options: Baseline motor, sensory, speech, or other residual deficits
questions.explanation: After a TIA or stroke, document baseline motor weakness or deficits so new postoperative deficits can be recognized.

questions.stem: A patient reports chronic neuralgia in the operative-side extremity. Which planning consequence is most appropriate?
options: Document the baseline symptoms and protect the extremity carefully during positioning
Treat regional anesthesia as absolutely contraindicated
Use inhalational induction to prevent symptom worsening
questions.explanation: Extremity neuralgia may require careful positioning to avoid worsening.

questions.stem: Which five findings increase concern for postoperative delirium or cognitive complications and therefore strengthen the need for a documented baseline? (Select 5)
questions.explanation: Risk factors include advanced age, baseline cognitive impairment, prior delirium, sensory impairment, polypharmacy, and alcohol or sedative use.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old with hearing loss, mild dementia, and 11 home medications presents for hip repair. Which postoperative complication is most strongly suggested by this cluster of preoperative findings?
questions.explanation: Age, cognitive impairment, sensory loss, and polypharmacy are listed delirium risk factors.

questions.stem: Which two patients most clearly require a detailed neurologic baseline because postoperative findings could otherwise be difficult to interpret? (Select 2)
options: A patient with diabetic neuropathy before a popliteal block
A patient scheduled for carotid endarterectomy
A healthy patient for cataract surgery
A healthy patient for dental extraction
A patient for laparoscopic cholecystectomy with no neurologic history
A healthy adult for hernia repair
questions.explanation: Detailed neuro exams are needed with regional anesthesia when deficits exist, carotid or vascular surgery, intracranial or spine surgery, recent stroke, high delirium risk, and altered mental status.

questions.stem: A patient with preexisting lower-extremity sensory loss is scheduled for regional anesthesia. Why is a detailed neurologic examination before the block especially important?
options: It establishes which deficits were present before the procedure for postoperative comparison
It proves regional anesthesia is contraindicated
It predicts local anesthetic systemic toxicity
questions.explanation: Documenting pre-existing deficits separates old findings from new injury after regional anesthesia.

questions.stem: A patient with a recent TIA is scheduled for carotid endarterectomy. Which preoperative step most directly improves detection of a new perioperative neurologic injury?
options: Perform and document a detailed neurologic baseline examination
Rely only on the neurologist's admission note
Delay surgery a fixed six weeks regardless of indication
questions.explanation: Carotid surgery and recent TIA are both listed situations needing a detailed neuro exam.

questions.stem: A patient is planned for MAC with local infiltration, and the surgeon expects no airway intervention. Which assessment should still be completed because the anesthetic may unexpectedly deepen or convert?
options: An airway evaluation only if conversion is already planned
No airway evaluation because the surgeon controls the airway
An airway evaluation only when general anesthesia is selected
questions.explanation: Airway assessment is essential regardless of anesthesia plan.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old drinks a pint of vodka daily and takes alprazolam 2 mg at night. He needs a far larger midazolam dose than expected, then becomes apneic after one more small dose. Which history should have shaped your dosing?
questions.explanation: Chronic alcohol and sedative use alter tolerance and response, requiring careful titration.

questions.stem: A patient with a subdural hematoma has new confusion and needs urgent surgery. Which preinduction examination is most important for later determining whether neurologic status changed perioperatively?
options: A six-week delay for neurologic recovery
questions.explanation: Altered mental status requires a detailed neuro exam to establish a baseline before surgery.

questions.stem: A thyroidectomy patient has Mallampati IV anatomy and limited cervical extension. Which preparation best addresses the anticipated difficulty before induction?
options: Have video laryngoscopy and the difficult-airway cart immediately available
Prepare a nasogastric tube, suction, and a standard blade only
Use supplemental oxygen by nasal cannula as the primary backup plan
Place an additional peripheral IV instead of preparing advanced airway equipment
questions.explanation: Anticipating a difficult airway means preparing a VL, positioning aids, and the difficult airway cart.

questions.stem: Which patient most needs a detailed preoperative neurologic baseline because postoperative mental-status changes would otherwise be difficult to interpret?
options: An 84-year-old with dementia and high delirium risk
A healthy 45-year-old for inguinal hernia repair
questions.explanation: Elderly patients at high risk of delirium need a detailed neuro baseline.

questions.stem: A patient has a chronic essential tremor. Which preoperative use of this finding is most important?
options: Establish the neurologic baseline and consider its implications for positioning or regional assessment
Use the tremor as a predictor of difficult laryngoscopy
Treat the tremor as a marker of malignant hyperthermia susceptibility
Consider regional anesthesia contraindicated in the affected limb
questions.explanation: Neuro disorders like essential tremor are part of the baseline neuro history.

questions.stem: A patient has reassuring Mallampati anatomy but a full beard, obesity, and limited cervical extension. Why should the airway examination integrate all of these findings?
options: Mask ventilation and tracheal intubation difficulty arise from different predictors, and several modest abnormalities can combine to increase rescue difficulty
Mallampati class alone predicts both mask ventilation and intubation
A beard affects laryngoscopy but not mask seal
Limited cervical extension matters only after extubation
questions.explanation: The airway exam predicts difficult mask ventilation and intubation, which guides equipment and backup plans.

questions.stem: A patient has recurrent migraines. Which history is most useful for distinguishing baseline symptoms from a perioperative neurologic problem?
options: Pattern or type, frequency, triggers, medications, and last episode
Presence or absence of aura alone
questions.explanation: The neuro slide asks about type, frequency, triggers, medications, and last episode.

questions.stem: A patient with cervical myelopathy is scheduled for laminectomy. Which additional preoperative examination is most important for interpreting postoperative neurologic findings?
options: A cardiac examination instead of neurologic assessment
A pulmonary examination instead of neurologic assessment
An airway examination instead of neurologic assessment
questions.explanation: Intracranial or spine surgery calls for a detailed neuro exam to document baseline deficits.

questions.stem: A patient has Mallampati II anatomy, three-fingerbreadth mouth opening, a full beard, and a short thick neck. Which conclusion best avoids false reassurance?
options: Several modest findings can combine to make ventilation or intubation difficult
Mallampati II makes the airway low risk regardless of the other findings
The beard is the only finding that materially affects the plan
Three-fingerbreadth mouth opening rules out difficult laryngoscopy
questions.explanation: Multiple minor abnormalities, such as a beard and short neck, can combine to make mask ventilation or intubation difficult.

questions.stem: A patient previously received extensive neck radiation and now has fixed, poorly compliant anterior neck tissues despite a modest Mallampati score. What is the key implication?
options: An acquired anatomic change may make airway management more difficult than the Mallampati score alone suggests
Radiation history is irrelevant if mouth opening is normal
The finding predicts only postoperative nausea
questions.explanation: Acquired anomalies include changes from radiation or surgery that can make the airway difficult.

questions.stem: An older adult takes numerous medications, including several with deliriogenic effects. Which delirium risk factor is most amenable to preoperative modification?
questions.explanation: Polypharmacy can be reduced before surgery by stopping or substituting deliriogenic drugs; age and baseline cognition cannot be changed.

questions.stem: A patient with long-standing action tremor takes propranolol and has no rigidity or resting tremor. Why should this history be documented before surgery?
options: It establishes a neurologic baseline and identifies a chronic beta-blocker that may affect perioperative medication planning
questions.explanation: Neurologic history includes CVA, Parkinson's disease, and essential tremor. Note the propranolol as a home beta-blocker.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic left-arm weakness after stroke is scheduled for a right-sided regional block. Which action best prevents a preexisting deficit from being misattributed to the anesthetic?
options: Document the baseline weakness before the block
Avoid the block solely because of the previous stroke
Document strength only after the block
Use general anesthesia to eliminate neurologic assessment concerns
questions.explanation: Regional anesthesia with pre-existing deficits is a listed situation; baseline documentation protects the patient and provider.

questions.stem: An older adult uses hearing aids and has significant visual impairment. Why should these devices and deficits matter to the perioperative plan?
options: Sensory impairment can worsen disorientation and increase delirium risk
questions.explanation: Hearing and vision impairment make orientation harder after surgery and are delirium risk factors. Keep glasses and hearing aids available in PACU.

questions.stem: A patient is scheduled for carpal tunnel release under local anesthesia with no planned sedation. Why is an airway assessment still appropriate?
options: Unexpected deterioration or conversion can still require airway rescue
Airway anatomy determines the local anesthetic dose
The surgeon requires an airway score for local anesthesia
questions.explanation: The airway is evaluated for every patient because any plan can require emergent airway control.

questions.stem: A 70-kg patient's resting oxygen consumption is about 245 mL/min. During an activity it rises to roughly 1,000 mL/min. Approximately what functional capacity does this represent?
questions.explanation: One MET is about 3.5 mL/kg/min, or about 245 mL/min for 70 kg. 1,000 mL/min ÷ 245 mL/min is about 4 METs.

questions.stem: A patient walks two miles and performs yard work without chest pain or dyspnea. Which inference about functional capacity is most appropriate?
options: Functional capacity is above 4 METs, suggesting useful cardiopulmonary reserve
Functional capacity is below 4 METs and mandates stress testing
Functional capacity cannot be estimated without CPET
Good functional capacity requires exceeding 10 METs
questions.explanation: More than 4 METs indicates good functional capacity and adequate cardiopulmonary reserve.

questions.stem: A patient climbs two flights of stairs daily without chest pain or dyspnea and has no unstable cardiac condition. Which interpretation best follows from that history?
options: Functional capacity is at least 4 METs, so additional cardiac testing is often unnecessary
Functional capacity is at least 4 METs, but age alone requires stress testing
Functional capacity is below 4 METs and requires cardiology referral
Functional capacity is indeterminate until echocardiography is performed
questions.explanation: Climbing two flights without symptoms shows ≥4 METs. Without unstable disease, additional testing is usually not required.

questions.stem: Which activity history most strongly reassures you that a patient can achieve at least moderate functional capacity without symptoms?
options: Scrubbing floors or moving heavy furniture
questions.explanation: Heavy housework, two flights of stairs or a hill, and moderate to strenuous activity show at least 4 METs.

questions.stem: A patient can perform basic activities of daily living but must stop halfway up one flight of stairs because of dyspnea. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Functional capacity is below 4 METs and warrants further risk assessment in the appropriate clinical context
Functional capacity is at least 4 METs because the patient is independent at home
Functional capacity is normal for age and adds no perioperative information
The dyspnea proves a pulmonary cause and lowers cardiac concern
questions.explanation: Failing stairs because of dyspnea means reduced capacity (<4 METs), which prompts further assessment per guidelines.

questions.stem: A patient reports activities corresponding to about 5 METs but has never undergone exercise testing. How should the recorded value be interpreted?
options: As a history-based estimate whose accuracy depends on the patient's report
As a directly measured oxygen-consumption value
As an objective measurement equivalent to CPET
As a value calculated from ejection fraction
questions.explanation: METs from history are a subjective estimate. Objective measures come from exercise testing or CPET.

questions.stem: A patient's arthritis makes activity history unreliable before an elevated-risk operation. Which test can objectively quantify functional capacity when such measurement would change management?
options: Cardiopulmonary exercise testing or an appropriate exercise test
questions.explanation: Exercise testing or CPET objectively measures functional capacity.

questions.stem: Two patients face the same elevated-risk procedure. One develops dyspnea after a short walk; the other performs strenuous activity without symptoms. What does the contrast contribute to risk assessment?
options: The first patient's limited functional capacity suggests less cardiopulmonary reserve and potentially greater perioperative risk
Functional capacity is irrelevant when the procedure is the same
The first patient necessarily has pulmonary rather than cardiac disease
The second patient requires more cardiac testing because strenuous activity raises myocardial demand
questions.explanation: Poor cardiopulmonary capacity is associated with increased perioperative risk.

questions.stem: Which two activities most strongly support functional capacity of at least 4 METs? (Select 2)
options: Walking one block on level ground
questions.explanation: Singles tennis and walking up a hill reach at least 4 METs. Walking one block on level ground, desk work, and washing dishes are below 4 METs.

questions.stem: An older adult cannot relate to stair-climbing questions. Which alternative history best estimates functional capacity using familiar daily activities?
options: Shopping, walking between stores, or pushing a mower
Hours of sleep and daytime naps
Driving distance and time behind the wheel
Meals per day and recent weight change
questions.explanation: Age-appropriate questions such as shopping, walking the mall, and pushing a mower estimate METs more reliably in older patients.

questions.stem: A patient climbs two flights of stairs without symptoms but has never had formal exercise testing. Why is that history still clinically useful?
options: It provides a practical estimate of functional capacity and cardiopulmonary reserve that can inform whether further testing is likely to add value
It replaces assessment for active cardiac symptoms
questions.explanation: Functional capacity is a surrogate marker of cardiopulmonary reserve before surgery.

questions.stem: A patient with diabetes and hypertension cannot walk far because of severe knee arthritis and is scheduled for an elevated-risk procedure. How should the limitation be interpreted?
options: Functional capacity is uncertain, so further risk assessment may be needed
Functional capacity should be assumed above 4 METs because the limitation is orthopedic
Functional capacity should be assumed below 4 METs and stress testing ordered automatically
Orthopedic limitation makes functional capacity irrelevant to perioperative assessment
questions.explanation: Capacity below 4 METs or unclear capacity prompts further cardiac risk assessment per guidelines.

questions.stem: A patient can climb stairs briskly but developed new chest pain at rest last week. Which finding should drive the preoperative decision?
options: The new rest pain because active cardiac symptoms override reassuring functional capacity
The stair-climbing ability because it demonstrates adequate reserve
The MET estimate because values above 4 exclude unstable disease
ASA physical status because it supersedes symptom history
questions.explanation: Good capacity usually means no further testing, provided there is no unstable cardiac disease. New rest angina is unstable.

questions.stem: A patient runs regularly but reports new chest pain at rest. What is the best next step?
options: Evaluate the active cardiac symptoms before elective surgery
Proceed because excellent exercise tolerance lowers risk enough
Proceed if a resting ECG is normal
Classify the patient as low risk based on exercise capacity alone
questions.explanation: Good capacity does not cancel active cardiac conditions like new rest angina. Those require evaluation.

questions.stem: A patient is ASA III with an RCRI of 1 and functional capacity around 5 METs. How should these measures be interpreted?
options: Together, because each describes a different part of perioperative risk
Use RCRI alone to decide whether surgery proceeds
Use METs alone to decide whether surgery proceeds
Use ASA status alone to decide whether surgery proceeds
questions.explanation: METs, RCRI, and ASA status are used together, since none fully captures risk alone.

questions.stem: A patient has functional capacity below 4 METs before an elevated-risk procedure. What does that threshold imply?
options: Further guideline-based cardiac risk assessment may be appropriate
Proceed because procedural risk is the only factor that matters
Proceed automatically if the RCRI is zero
Choose regional anesthesia instead of further assessment
questions.explanation: Reduced capacity prompts further cardiac risk assessment, which may include testing or consultation.

questions.stem: A patient swims laps and performs heavy housework without chest pain or dyspnea. How should this history influence preoperative cardiac assessment?
options: It supports at least moderate functional capacity, but active cardiac symptoms and overall procedural risk still take precedence
It proves coronary disease is absent
It mandates CPET because the activities are strenuous
It eliminates the need to ask about new cardiac symptoms
questions.explanation: Heavy household work and swimming are ≥4 MET activities.

questions.stem: A patient says he 'walks a lot,' but collateral history reveals dyspnea after half a block. Which limitation of history-based MET estimation does this illustrate?
options: It is subjective and depends on the accuracy of reported activity
It is an objective value derived from echocardiography
It is validated only in pediatric patients
It predicts pulmonary complications but not cardiovascular risk
questions.explanation: METs from history are subjective and can be over- or underestimated; objective testing such as CPET is more reliable.

questions.stem: Which history most strongly suggests functional capacity below the commonly used 4-MET threshold?
options: Stopping during a single flight of stairs because of dyspnea
Climbing one flight slowly without symptoms
questions.explanation: Inability to climb stairs due to fatigue and dyspnea indicates less than 4 METs, or poor capacity.

questions.stem: A patient carries groceries up two flights of stairs without symptoms and has no active cardiac condition. What is the most useful implication?
options: The history supports adequate functional capacity and may reduce the value of additional cardiac testing when no other indication exists
Stress testing is mandatory because stairs are not objective
The history excludes coronary artery disease
Age alone determines whether cardiology consultation is required
questions.explanation: More than 4 METs suggests sufficient cardiopulmonary reserve; testing is usually not needed without active disease.

questions.stem: A patient had a drug-eluting coronary stent placed 4 months ago and now needs elective noncardiac surgery. Which plan best reflects the lecture's timing and antiplatelet principles?
options: Proceed if the 3–6 month interval is acceptable and continue aspirin
Proceed but stop aspirin 7 days before surgery
Delay 12 months and stop all antiplatelet therapy
Proceed after stopping dual antiplatelet therapy for 60 days
questions.explanation: Elective surgery after a DES is acceptable at 3–6 months with aspirin continued to reduce stent thrombosis.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient had a bare-metal coronary stent placed 5 weeks ago and now requests elective hernia repair. How should the timing be interpreted?
options: The interval exceeds 30 days, so timing is acceptable by the lecture rule
Elective surgery must wait at least 6 months
Elective surgery must wait at least 12 months
Seven days is sufficient after any coronary stent
questions.explanation: Elective surgery can proceed more than 30 days after a bare metal stent.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient had a myocardial infarction 5 weeks ago that was managed medically without PCI or CABG. Which timing principle applies to elective surgery?
options: Delay until at least 60 days after the MI
Proceed because more than 30 days have passed
Proceed if functional capacity exceeds 4 METs
questions.explanation: After an MI managed without intervention, wait at least 60 days before elective surgery.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient had CABG 4 months ago and requests elective shoulder replacement. Which timing recommendation best follows from the lecture?
options: Delay until more than 6 months after CABG
Proceed after 3 months if aspirin is continued
questions.explanation: Elective surgery should wait more than 6 months after CABG.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient had a drug-eluting stent placed 7 weeks ago and takes aspirin plus clopidogrel. The surgeon proposes stopping both drugs for elective surgery next week. Which concern should take priority?
options: Premature interruption of antiplatelet therapy with very recent DES placement increases stent-thrombosis risk
Stopping both drugs for 5 days makes the procedure acceptable
Restarting dual antiplatelet therapy in PACU removes the excess risk
A normal ECG would make early surgery acceptable
questions.explanation: DES patients are on DAPT and elective surgery is delayed 3–6 months with aspirin continued. Stopping DAPT early risks stent thrombosis.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient develops perioperative myocardial injury during profound anemia and hypotension without evidence of acute plaque rupture. Which mechanism best explains the event?
options: Acute coronary plaque rupture with thrombosis
Sudden cardiac death without biomarker evidence
questions.explanation: Type II MI results from supply-demand imbalance, such as anemia or sepsis hypotension, and is not fixed by PCI.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Which five findings increase this vascular-surgery patient's baseline risk for ischemic heart disease? (Select 5)
questions.explanation: IHD risk factors include age, smoking, diabetes, hypertension, and PVD. Hypothyroidism is not on this list.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: One patient has unchanged exertional angina for three years; another developed new rest angina twice this week. Which preoperative distinction matters most?
options: The stable patient may proceed based on overall risk, while the patient with new rest angina needs cardiac evaluation first
Both patients require the same cardiac evaluation before surgery
Both may proceed because both have known angina
The patient with rest angina may proceed while the stable patient requires evaluation
questions.explanation: Stable angina is not an active condition, but new rest angina is unstable and needs evaluation before elective surgery.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient with poor functional capacity has an abnormal noninvasive ischemia study before major vascular surgery, and the result will change management. Which test can directly define coronary anatomy when further invasive evaluation is indicated?
questions.explanation: Cardiac catheterization provides definitive information about coronary anatomy.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient requires ischemia evaluation but cannot exercise because of severe arthritis. Which testing strategy best preserves the purpose of stress testing?
options: Pharmacologic stress using an agent such as dobutamine or adenosine
Treadmill testing at a very low workload
questions.explanation: Patients who cannot exercise can have pharmacologic stress testing with dipyridamole, adenosine, or dobutamine.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient with known CAD says a cardiologist evaluated him last month. Which next step yields the most actionable perioperative information?
options: Obtain the recent cardiology assessment and recommendations
Ask only whether the patient takes a statin
Order a chest radiograph if none was obtained this year
questions.explanation: A recent cardiology note or clearance gives current function, testing, and recommendations that guide your plan.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Two patients face the same colectomy; one has EF 55% and the other EF 30%. Which consequence is most important for the lower-EF patient?
options: Greater perioperative risk with implications for hemodynamic management
No important difference unless the surgery is cardiac
Lower anesthetic requirements without a change in overall risk
Relevance only if cardiopulmonary bypass is planned
questions.explanation: An EF below 40% signals higher perioperative risk and affects drug choice, monitoring, and fluid management.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Repeated preoperative blood pressures average 148/94 mmHg without acute symptoms. Which classification describes the pressure itself?
questions.explanation: Stage 2 is ≥140/≥90. Stage 1 is 130–139/80–89, and elevated is 120–129/<80.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient presents for elective surgery with BP 162/98 mmHg, no symptoms, and no evidence of end-organ injury. Which interpretation best follows from the lecture?
options: A pressure below 180/110 mmHg is not by itself an independent predictor of perioperative cardiovascular complications
Any pressure above 140/90 mmHg requires cancellation
Stage 2 hypertension automatically requires cardiology consultation
A systolic pressure above 160 mmHg requires an immediate beta-blocker bolus
questions.explanation: The slide states <180/<110 is not an independent predictor of CV complications. Assess end-organ damage and symptoms.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient presents with BP 168/98 mmHg before surgery. Which three findings most directly determine whether this represents uncomplicated chronic hypertension or a higher-risk perioperative problem? (Select 3)
options: Symptoms such as syncope or dizziness
Antihypertensive medications, doses, and last dose time
Blood pressure at the last dental visit
Whether blood pressure is usually higher at night
questions.explanation: Hypertension assessment focuses on end-organ dysfunction, symptoms, and the medication list with timing.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient took lisinopril, amlodipine, metoprolol, and chlorthalidone on the morning of surgery. Why is the exact medication list and timing clinically important before induction?
options: It helps anticipate peri-induction hemodynamic responses
questions.explanation: Multiple agents taken the same morning, especially ACE inhibitors and diuretics, predict hypotension after induction.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient had a drug-eluting coronary stent 8 months ago and takes aspirin alone. What is the most important preoperative issue before deciding whether aspirin should be interrupted?
options: Balance surgical bleeding risk against coronary thrombotic risk using the stent history and current indication
Stop aspirin routinely because more than 6 months have passed
Restart dual antiplatelet therapy solely for surgery
Delay every elective operation until 12 months after any drug-eluting stent
questions.explanation: After 3–6 months with a DES, elective surgery can proceed with aspirin continued.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient with remote myocardial infarction presents for colectomy. Which cardiac-assessment goal is most useful for building the anesthetic plan?
options: Establish baseline function, identify active disease, estimate risk, and plan monitoring
Diagnose every possible coronary lesion before surgery
Obtain cardiology clearance for any history of CAD
Avoid elective surgery in all patients with previous MI
questions.explanation: Cardiac assessment establishes baseline function, identifies active conditions, estimates risk, and guides monitoring and optimization.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Which four findings should interrupt routine elective-surgery planning until further cardiac evaluation is considered? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Red flags include active angina, recent MI, decompensated HF, symptomatic arrhythmia, severe symptomatic valvular disease, unexplained syncope, and new symptoms.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Four patients with similar coronary disease are scheduled for different procedures. Which operation contributes the greatest additional cardiac stress from procedural risk?
options: Superficial skin excision under local anesthesia
questions.explanation: Major vascular and prolonged intrathoracic or intra-abdominal procedures are high cardiac risk.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient with CAD and poor functional capacity is scheduled for one of four procedures. Which operation adds the least procedural cardiac risk?
questions.explanation: Cataract surgery is low cardiac risk; major vascular and prolonged intrathoracic or intra-abdominal cases are high risk.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A cardiology note from two years ago describes stable disease, but the patient now reports worsening exertional dyspnea. Which information should drive today's decision?
options: The new symptom pattern, prompting updated cardiac evaluation before elective surgery
The old cardiology note because it remains in the chart
The option to use regional anesthesia instead of further evaluation
A single normal resting ECG obtained this morning
questions.explanation: New or worsening symptoms are red flags; a recent cardiology note or evaluation is needed.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient with prior MI takes amiodarone. Which ECG review is most complete for identifying findings that could alter the anesthetic plan?
options: Rhythm, conduction, prior infarct patterns, ischemic changes, and QT interval
Axis and voltage only because rhythm will be monitored intraoperatively
Rate and rhythm only because ischemia requires echocardiography
P waves and QRS width only because QT is not clinically relevant
questions.explanation: ECG review covers rhythm, conduction, prior infarct, ischemic changes, QT (relevant with amiodarone), and pacing.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient had a bare-metal coronary stent placed 3 weeks ago and requests elective cholecystectomy. Which timing issue should prevent routine progression to surgery?
options: The interval is still under the lecture's 30-day minimum after BMS placement
The case may proceed if dual antiplatelet therapy is continued
The case may proceed if aspirin is stopped
The case must be delayed 6 months, identical to CABG
questions.explanation: BMS requires >30 days before elective surgery.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient is 4 months after PCI and still requires aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor. Which detail is most important when judging the hazard of interrupting therapy for elective surgery?
options: The stent type, indication for PCI, and required duration of antiplatelet therapy
Whether the infarct was anterior or inferior
Whether the patient has ever received general anesthesia
questions.explanation: Patients with drug-eluting stents are maintained on DAPT, which shapes surgical timing.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Which preoperative profile most strongly supports proceeding to an intermediate-risk operation without additional cardiac testing?
options: Regular rhythm, no JVD, controlled blood pressure, and functional capacity above 4 METs
Irregular rhythm with a holosystolic murmur and JVD
Tachycardia with S3 and pulmonary crackles
Bradycardia with gallop and peripheral edema
questions.explanation: A normal exam, good capacity, controlled hypertension, and no active conditions support proceeding without more testing.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient has unchanged exertional angina for three years, functional capacity above 4 METs, and no new symptoms. Which distinction is most important?
options: Stable symptoms with adequate functional capacity do not represent an active cardiac condition
Any angina requires urgent catheterization before elective surgery
Chronic beta-blockade should be stopped to prevent bradycardia
Elective surgery must be delayed six months
questions.explanation: Stable angina with good capacity and no change is not an active condition.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Which two physical findings most strongly suggest volume-overloaded heart failure during preoperative assessment? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Heart failure signs include JVD, crackles, peripheral edema, hepatomegaly, and fluid overload.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient had an MI treated with PCI 2 months ago. Which missing procedural detail most directly determines whether the lecture's elective-surgery timing threshold has been met?
options: Whether the PCI used a bare-metal or drug-eluting stent
Whether the infarct was inferior or anterior
Whether the patient required hospital admission
questions.explanation: Timing rules differ for BMS (>30 days) and DES (3–6 months).
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Two patients both have BP 168/98 mmHg. One is asymptomatic; the other has headache, blurred vision, and new proteinuria. Why should the second patient be treated differently in the risk assessment?
options: The symptoms and proteinuria suggest end-organ involvement
The asymptomatic patient carries greater perioperative risk
Identical pressures imply identical risk regardless of symptoms
End-organ symptoms matter only above 200/120 mmHg
questions.explanation: Symptoms of end-organ dysfunction raise risk and may warrant delay, while asymptomatic BP under 180/110 does not independently predict risk.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient with long-standing hypertension has a preoperative pressure of 154/92 mmHg but no acute symptoms. Why does the history still matter even if this single value does not mandate cancellation?
options: Chronic hypertension may reflect target-organ disease and altered cardiovascular reserve that affect perioperative management
Any chronic hypertension independently requires cancellation
The diagnosis eliminates the need to assess symptoms
questions.explanation: Hypertension is extremely common and contributes to about half a million deaths per year.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Repeated preoperative blood pressures average 134/86 mmHg. Which category best matches those values?
questions.explanation: Stage 1 is 130–139/80–89. Elevated is 120–129 with diastolic under 80.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Four patients with valve disease are scheduled for elective noncardiac surgery. Which lesion creates the greatest concern for perioperative hemodynamic collapse?
questions.explanation: Severe AS (area under 1 cm²) carries the greatest concern because of perioperative sudden death risk.

questions.stem: An echocardiogram shows aortic valve area 0.8 cm², mean gradient 44 mmHg, and peak velocity 4.2 m/s. Which interpretation best connects the measurements to perioperative risk?
options: The findings meet severe aortic stenosis criteria and indicate high perioperative risk
The findings represent moderate aortic stenosis with low perioperative risk
The findings represent mild aortic stenosis with no special precautions
The findings show aortic sclerosis without stenosis
questions.explanation: Valve area under 1.0 cm² defines severe AS, which carries high risk of hemodynamic collapse and sudden death.

questions.stem: An echocardiogram shows aortic jet velocity 4.3 m/s and mean gradient 46 mmHg. Which severity category is supported by both measurements?
questions.explanation: Velocity ≥4 m/s and gradient ≥40 mmHg meet severe criteria.

questions.stem: An echocardiogram shows aortic jet velocity 3.4 m/s, mean gradient 28 mmHg, and valve area 1.2 cm². Which severity category is most consistent across all three measurements?
questions.explanation: Moderate AS is velocity 3.0–3.9, gradient 20–39, and area 1.0–1.5 cm².

questions.stem: A patient with severe aortic stenosis is scheduled for major surgery. Which physiologic problem makes abrupt anesthetic-induced hypotension especially dangerous?
options: A fixed outflow obstruction limits the ability to increase forward flow when coronary perfusion pressure falls
The ventricle can easily increase stroke volume to compensate
Severe aortic stenosis primarily causes excessive vasodilation
Tachycardia reliably improves diastolic filling and coronary perfusion
questions.explanation: The note says severe AS means high risk of an intraoperative event.

questions.stem: A patient with known valvular disease presents for elective hip replacement. Which information most directly defines the lesion's current severity and physiologic significance?
options: Current symptoms plus echocardiography and relevant catheterization data
Murmur description and ECG findings alone
questions.explanation: Valvular disease assessment relies on echo, cath data, and symptoms.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old with exertional dyspnea has a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border. Which lesion best fits both the timing and location?
questions.explanation: MR and AS are systolic (MRASS); MS and AR are diastolic (MSARD). A RUSB crescendo-decrescendo murmur suggests AS.

questions.stem: A holosystolic murmur is loudest at the apex and radiates toward the axilla. Which lesion is most likely?
questions.explanation: MR is holosystolic at the apex and radiates to the axilla.

questions.stem: A midsystolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur is heard at the second right interspace and radiates to the carotids. Which lesion best matches this pattern?
questions.explanation: AS produces a crescendo-decrescendo midsystolic murmur at the second interspace radiating to the carotids.

questions.stem: A low-pitched middiastolic rumble with an opening snap is heard at the apex. Which lesion is most likely?
questions.explanation: MS produces an opening snap and middiastolic rumble at the apex.

questions.stem: A systolic murmur becomes louder with standing or Valsalva and softer with squatting. Which lesion is most consistent with this preload-sensitive pattern?
questions.explanation: HCM and MVP increase with Valsalva/standing; AS decreases with Valsalva. The table lists HCM as midsystolic at the apex/LLSB.

questions.stem: A patient has clinical heart failure but an ejection fraction of 58%. Which classification best describes the ventricular phenotype?
options: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
Heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction
Normal cardiac function with no heart failure
questions.explanation: HFpEF is EF above 50% and lower risk than HFrEF (EF under about 49%).

questions.stem: Two patients with heart failure face the same operation; one has EF 58% and the other EF 32%. Which feature most strongly identifies the higher-risk patient?
options: Reduced EF of 32% consistent with HFrEF
Preserved EF of 58% consistent with HFpEF
The risks are equivalent because both have heart failure
Ejection fraction does not influence perioperative risk
questions.explanation: HFrEF carries higher perioperative risk than HFpEF.

questions.stem: Which four findings most strongly support decompensated left-ventricular dysfunction before surgery? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Signs of LV dysfunction include dyspnea, pulmonary edema, tachypnea, tachycardia, and JVD.

questions.stem: A patient has insulin-treated diabetes, creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, prior myocardial infarction, and is scheduled for open colectomy. What RCRI score results from those findings?
questions.explanation: Insulin-treated diabetes, creatinine above 2.0, ischemic heart disease, and intraperitoneal surgery each add 1 point, for 4.

questions.stem: A patient has creatinine 2.3 mg/dL before elevated-risk noncardiac surgery. How does this affect the classic RCRI?
options: It does not count unless creatinine exceeds 3.0 mg/dL
It counts only if dialysis is required
questions.explanation: The RCRI renal criterion is creatinine above 2.0 mg/dL.

questions.stem: Two patients with diabetes undergo the same operation. One uses metformin only; the other requires basal-bolus insulin. Which difference changes the classic RCRI?
options: Insulin treatment adds the diabetes criterion; metformin treatment alone does not
Both receive the same diabetes point
Only metformin treatment adds the criterion
questions.explanation: Only diabetes requiring insulin earns an RCRI point.

questions.stem: A patient uses insulin, has prior stroke, creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, and is scheduled for open AAA repair. What is the RCRI score?
questions.explanation: Insulin DM (1), cerebrovascular disease (1), Cr >2.0 (1), suprainguinal vascular surgery (1) = 4.

questions.stem: A patient's classic RCRI score is 3. How should the score be used?
options: As one estimate of cardiac risk that should be integrated with current symptoms, functional capacity, procedure, and other clinical factors
As a precise individualized probability that replaces clinical assessment
As a reason to cancel surgery automatically
As a tool that already incorporates frailty and functional capacity

questions.stem: A patient with no classic RCRI clinical risk factors is scheduled for intraperitoneal surgery. How does the procedure affect the score?
options: The high-risk-surgery criterion adds one point
The procedure adds no points because only patient diseases count
All abdominal surgery adds two points
Only vascular surgery can add a procedural point
questions.explanation: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is intraperitoneal, which is 1 RCRI point. With no other factors, her score is 1 and her MACE risk is about 1.0%.

questions.stem: Which THREE operations satisfy the classic RCRI high-risk-surgery category? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: High-risk surgery includes intraperitoneal, intrathoracic, or suprainguinal vascular procedures.

questions.stem: A patient with ischemic heart disease and prior heart failure is scheduled for intraperitoneal surgery. What classic RCRI score results from those three findings?
questions.explanation: IHD (1), CHF (1), and intraperitoneal surgery (1) = 3.

questions.stem: A patient has RCRI 0, poor stair-climbing tolerance from dyspnea, and ASA III status. Why is it unsafe to stop the assessment at the RCRI score?
options: RCRI must be interpreted alongside functional capacity and overall disease burden
RCRI predicts pulmonary rather than cardiac outcomes
RCRI applies only to cardiac surgery
RCRI already contains METs and ASA status
questions.explanation: RCRI is not a standalone tool; poor functional capacity and ASA status add important information.

questions.stem: A patient has a prior episode of pulmonary edema and now has an S3 with jugular venous distension. Which RCRI criterion is satisfied?
questions.explanation: A history or signs of heart failure satisfy the RCRI congestive heart failure criterion.

questions.stem: A patient with prior rheumatic fever has a low-pitched diastolic rumble at the apex. Which lesion best fits the finding?
questions.explanation: MS and AR are diastolic (MSARD). Rheumatic disease commonly causes mitral stenosis.

questions.stem: A blowing holodiastolic murmur is heard along the left sternal border in a patient with wide pulse pressure. Which lesion is most likely?
questions.explanation: Aortic insufficiency produces a holodiastolic murmur at the left parasternal spaces with a wide pulse pressure.

questions.stem: A patient has a midsystolic click followed by a late systolic murmur that becomes earlier with standing. Which lesion best fits?
questions.explanation: A midsystolic click followed by a late systolic murmur is characteristic of mitral valve prolapse.

questions.stem: A patient has a new murmur and exertional dyspnea before elective surgery. Which next step is more useful than identifying whether aortic or mitral lesions are statistically more common?
options: Characterize the murmur, symptoms, and current valve severity because those findings determine perioperative significance
Assume an aortic lesion because it is common
Assume a mitral lesion because it is common
Proceed without further assessment because prevalence does not affect management
questions.explanation: Aortic and mitral lesions are most common in adults.

questions.stem: A patient with previously severe aortic stenosis has only a 2-year-old echocardiogram and is now scheduled for elective hip replacement. Which information is most important before deciding whether to proceed?
options: Current symptoms plus updated echo and relevant catheterization data
Today's murmur intensity and blood pressure alone
Planned use of spinal anesthesia alone
questions.explanation: Severe AS is high risk. Current echo, cath data, and symptoms guide whether and how to proceed; spinal is often avoided.

questions.stem: A patient with prior myocardial infarction is scheduled for suprainguinal vascular surgery and has no other classic RCRI factors. What score results?
questions.explanation: Ischemic heart disease and high-risk surgery each add 1 point, for a score of 2 and about 2.4% MACE risk.

questions.stem: A patient had a transient ischemic attack 6 months ago with complete recovery. Which RCRI criterion does that history satisfy?
questions.explanation: Prior stroke or TIA counts as cerebrovascular disease in the RCRI.

questions.stem: Which preoperative rhythm finding is most compatible with proceeding to elective surgery when the patient is otherwise stable?
options: New atrial fibrillation with ventricular rate 140
Nonsustained ventricular tachycardia with family history of sudden death
questions.explanation: Rate-controlled AF, PVCs, and PACs are generally benign.

questions.stem: Which arrhythmia history should raise the greatest concern before elective surgery?
options: SVT requiring flecainide plus a family history of sudden death
questions.explanation: SVT requiring antiarrhythmics, or a family history of sudden death, labels a history potentially malignant. Rate-controlled AF, PACs, and isolated PVCs are generally benign.

questions.stem: A patient has new palpitations and atrial fibrillation with ventricular rate 132 two days before elective knee replacement. What should happen before surgery?
options: Evaluate the new arrhythmia before proceeding
Proceed and manage the rate intraoperatively
